changes.title: Frontier conflict displays

changes.title: A shrine turned exhibition complex
changes.body: 83,000 square metres of new floor space, built for exhibitions rather than remembrance, on ground consecrated to 103,000 names.

hero.lede: The Memorial is not a political vehicle. It is our national shrine, the grave of 103,000 names. Now they want to fill it with activism and contested history. Our fallen cannot object.

happened.heading: A decision no Australian was asked about
body: In August 2022, behind closed doors, the Council of the Australian War Memorial decided to build a gallery inside the Memorial devoted to anti-colonial activism, and contested history.

There was no Act of Parliament. There was no public consultation. There was no legal advice. Asked at Senate Estimates whether the Council would even check that it had the power, the Memorial's Director said there were no plans to.

The decision was recorded in a single paragraph of a council minute. Those minutes did not surface for nine months, and only then because a Senator asked for them. When a member of the public later asked for the policy under Freedom of Information, the Memorial replied that no documents existed. On review, it reversed and confirmed the policy does exist.
The gallery is now confirmed. Roughly 200 square metres, the size of a singles tennis court, on the main concourse at the entrance. The Director calls it "the next step."

responsible.heading: Kim Beazley knows better than this
body: Kim Beazley has been Minister for Defence. He has been Australia's Ambassador to the United States. He has been Governor of Western Australia. He is the son of a man this country respected. There is no one in public life who better understands what the Memorial is for, and the lives it honours.

He is the decision's loudest public advocate. On national radio he dismissed the Memorial's telling of our history as a fiction, and he has promised to use the Memorial itself to make Australians accept his version of the story. His words are on the record, at the bottom of this page.
responsible.emBody: That is a man describing the nation's shrine as his to instruct us with.
responsible.close: Kim Beazley can be remembered as a Defence Minister and Governor. Or he can be remembered as the man who attempted to introduce activism into Australia's history. He cannot get away with it.
responsible.cta: Tell him no. Sign the petition.

items.title: It is sacred, not a museum.
items.body: The Memorial is sacred ground. It bears the names of 103,000 Australians who died serving this country, and it is where their families come to mourn. Introducing activism into that space is not something a nation does lightly. This history already has a home: the National Museum of Australia, the Australian Museum, and the $316.5 million Ngurra precinct. It is not this one.

items.title: It was done by stealth.
items.body: No Act. No consultation. No legal advice. A single paragraph in a minute, nine months to release, and an FOI answer that said no documents existed until it was challenged. Whatever you think of our history, our national memorial should not change in secret.

items.title: It redefined what Australia is.
items.body: The controversial historians behind this have been explicit. One has proposed placing a second tomb beside the Tomb of the Unknown Australian Soldier, so that "those who fought for empire would be at rest with those who fought against the empire." The campaign's own website calls for names added to the Roll of Honour. The same historian co-wrote a book asking whether it is "not now time for Australia to cast aside" the Anzac legend. This is not an addition to Anzac. It is a replacement for it.

items.title: It is being built into a $548 million job.
items.body: The Memorial's redevelopment has been funded at $548.7 million, the largest works programme in its history. The frontier galleries are one part of that spend, and they are the part that changes what the building says about Australia. Building them in at this scale is what makes them permanent. Three in four Australians say the money would be better spent on health, education and veterans' services. Fewer than one in five support putting frontier conflict in the Memorial at all.

notSaying.heading: Where it belongs, and who decides
body: This is not an argument about whether the history is true. It is an argument about where it belongs, and about who gets to decide.

In 2018 the Memorial's own Director wrote that the story "should be told at the National Museum of Australia, not the Australian War Memorial." That is our position. It was the Memorial's position too, until the Council changed its mind without changing the law.

variations.subject: The War Memorial is not the Council's to change
variations.body:
Dear Minister,

I am writing about the decision of the Council of the Australian War Memorial to place colonial frontier conflict displays inside the Memorial.

The Memorial is governed by an Act of Parliament that covers war and warlike operations by the Defence Force. The Council made this change without an Act of Parliament, without public consultation, and without taking legal advice on whether it had the power at all.

I ask you to maintain the sanctity of the Australian War Memorial by:

1. Halting and removing the frontier conflicts and other contested history that contravene the War Memorial's governing Act.
2. Abstaining from further historical revisions without approval from the Parliament of Australia.

I would appreciate a response setting out your position.

Yours sincerely,

donate.heading: Australians do not even know this is happening. You can make the difference.
body: They did this quietly in secret, and quiet is how it stays unless you help break the silence.

They have a $548 million works programme, a national institution, and the advantage of already being inside the building. We have no member of parliament, no broadcaster and no public funding. What we have is everyday Australians and the truth. Neither of those reaches anyone for free.

Only one Australian in ten has heard that any of this is happening. That silence is not bad luck. It is the strategy, and it is exactly why they expect to get away with it. Every dollar you give buys the one thing that beats it: another Australian who finds out in time to object.

$35 puts the story in front of 1,400 people. $265 buys a full page in a regional paper. $1,500 puts it on a Canberra billboard for a month. That is the entire campaign. There is nothing else funding this and no one else coming.

issue.heading: A shrine, not a soapbox.
issue.lede: A $548 million works programme is rebuilding Australia's national shrine, and activist history is being built into it, rewriting what the Memorial says about Australia and our fallen.
issue.proseHeading: Our shrine is NOT for politics or activism.
prose: The Memorial was built to one purpose: to hold the record of Australians who died serving the Commonwealth. Charles Bean called it the grave they never had. For 85 years, governments of both stripes kept faith with that purpose.

That has changed. Under the works programme, exhibition floor space is being multiplied, curatorial plans introduce frontier conflict displays and "contested history" framing, and the ground beneath the Parade Ground has been excavated. None of it was ever put to Australians as a whole. Now it finally is.

Make no mistake about why. The activists pushing these changes want to delegitimise Australia and the fact of its settlement, and the nation's shrine is the most sacred platform they can seize for that cause.

notAWar.heading: The frontier conflicts were not a war.
body: Describing the frontier conflicts as a war is activist revision, not history. We reject the false history and narrative that this country was engaged in a widespread frontier war.

In reality, Australia was settled relatively peacefully compared with other countries: research so far suggests only seven British soldiers were killed during Australia's colonisation. Contested claims like these belong in museums and history books, not in the nation's shrine.

about.heading: Ordinary Australians.
about.lede: Veterans, families of the fallen, and people who simply stood at a dawn service once and understood what the quiet was for.
who: Defend Sacred Ground began around kitchen tables in Canberra and grew through RSL halls, veterans' groups, and families with a name on the Roll of Honour. We hold no office, take no party's money, and want nothing for ourselves.

We want one thing: that the Australian War Memorial remains what it was built to be, a place that honours Australians who died serving the Commonwealth, free of activism and contested history. When the plans are withdrawn, this campaign winds itself up.

facts: The Australian War Memorial is undergoing a redevelopment budgeted at $548.7 million, and a reinterpretation of Australia's history is part of that program.
The changes were approved by the Australian War Memorial Council, chaired by Kim Beazley.
They were not put to the public before they were approved.
The campaign asks for the works to be paused, the decisions published in full, and the Memorial kept as a place of commemoration.
media.ctaBody: Tell us what you need and when you need it by. We would rather help you get it right than read a correction.

won.heading: You did this.
won.lede: The works are paused. That happened because tens of thousands of Australians refused to let it go through quietly.
body: It was not a change of heart. It was a change of arithmetic. Enough people signed, wrote and gave that the cost of pressing on became higher than the cost of stopping.
Nothing about it is permanent yet. A pause is a pause, and the same Council that approved this once can approve it again the moment the attention moves on.
won.nextBody: The decisions still have not been published in full, and until they are nobody can say what else was approved. That is the next thing.
